summary: Defines MIB objects extending the alarm threshold capabilities of the RMON MIB in RFC 2819 so they can monitor objects using the 64-bit counter data type, which the original alarms could not handle well.

eli5.summary: Counters on fast links grow so large that the old alarm could not follow them. This note adds an alarm bell that works with much bigger numbers.

questions: what is the rmon hc alarm mib
subtitle: A MIB that lets RMON-style rising and falling threshold alarms watch 64-bit counters.

tldr.problem: The RMON-1 alarm mechanism is specific to 32-bit objects and cannot properly monitor Counter64 objects, whose use is increasing as network interfaces get faster.
tldr.mechanism: The HC-ALARM MIB adds an hcAlarmTable that copies most of the RMON-1 alarmTable but splits each 64-bit threshold into high and low 32-bit halves, plus a capabilities object and two notifications, hcRisingAlarm and hcFallingAlarm.
tldr.outcome: Agents can set rising and falling thresholds on objects such as ifHCInOctets and ifHCOutOctets. The extension is independent of the existing RMON-1 alarm mechanisms.

today: RFC 3434 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the alarm group of RFC 2819 rather than replacing it.

sections.title: Why 64-bit Alarms Are Needed
sections.content:
RMON-1 has an alarm mechanism, but its alarmTable and notifications are specific to 32-bit objects and cannot properly monitor Counter64 objects. Use of Counter64 is rising partly because interface speeds are rising. The RFC quotes RFC 2863: a 10Mbs stream of back-to-back full-size packets makes ifInOctets wrap in just over 57 minutes, at 100Mbs the minimum wrap time is 5.7 minutes, and at 1Gbs it is 34 seconds.

Two of the most popular variables for thresholds are ifInOctets and ifOutOctets, so there is a growing need to threshold their 64-bit versions, ifHCInOctets and ifHCOutOctets. The RMON-1 Alarm Group is implemented by all RMON probes and by SNMP agents in many other devices, so the RFC calls this extension the easiest, simplest and most compatible way to overcome the lack of 64-bit support.
sections.eli5: On fast connections a small counter fills up and starts over in seconds. A bigger counter needs a bigger alarm.

sections.title: MIB Structure
sections.content:
The HC-ALARM MIB is meant for RMON probes, which may be stand-alone or co-located with devices such as ethernet switches and repeaters. Its functionality is a superset of the RMON-1 Alarm Group. The RFC says RMON-1's alarms might one day be deprecated in its favour, but not before this document or a successor reaches the same standardization state as RMON-1.

The MIB has three groups.

  • hcAlarmControlObjects: configures alarms for high capacity object instances.
  • hcAlarmCapabilities: describes the alarm capabilities the agent provides.
  • hcAlarmNotifications: new rising and falling threshold notifications.

Like RMON-1's alarmTable, the new hcAlarmTable feeds the shared RMON-1 eventTable, which in turn produces the notifications.
sections.eli5: There is a settings group, a group that says what the device can do, and a group that rings the bells.

sections.title: The High Capacity Alarm Table
sections.content:
A management station configures alarms on Counter64 or CounterBasedGauge64 objects by setting up the hcAlarmTable much as it would RMON-1's alarmTable. Many objects are cloned with new names, such as hcAlarmInterval, hcAlarmVariable, hcAlarmSampleType, hcAlarmStartupAlarm, the two event indexes, hcAlarmOwner and hcAlarmStatus. This is because the wording of some alarmTable descriptions ties them to that table.

The value and the thresholds are different. The sampled value is hcAlarmAbsValue with a companion hcAlarmValueStatus. Each threshold is split into a Lo and a Hi 32-bit object plus a status object, combined as Lo + (Hi * 2^32).

The table also differs from alarmTable in these ways:

  • Counter64 based objects are thresholded properly.
  • An entry is not destroyed if the sampled instance is unavailable during a polling interval.
  • The RowStatus textual convention is used instead of EntryStatus for hcAlarmStatus.
  • Non-volatile storage is explicitly controlled with a StorageType parameter.
  • A counter, hcAlarmValueFailedAttempts, records how many times the variable could not be retrieved.
sections.eli5: Big numbers are written in two halves and glued together. The alarm also keeps count of the times it could not check the thing it was watching.

sections.title: Sampling and Thresholds
sections.content:
hcAlarmInterval is the number of seconds (1 to 2147483647) between samples. hcAlarmVariable points at the variable to sample; only variables that resolve to an ASN.1 integer type such as Integer32, Counter32, Counter64, Gauge or TimeTicks may be sampled.

hcAlarmSampleType is either absoluteValue(1), comparing the variable directly with the thresholds, or deltaValue(2), comparing the difference from the previous sample. For delta sampling the interval should be short enough that the variable is very unlikely to change by more than 2^63 - 1 in one interval. If the previous sample could not be obtained, no delta is possible and hcAlarmValueStatus is valueNotAvailable(1). The textual convention HcValueStatus also distinguishes valuePositive(2) and valueNegative(3), so the absolute value can carry a sign.

An event fires when the sampled value reaches the rising threshold having been below it at the last sample, and a later rising event waits until the value has fallen below that threshold. hcAlarmStartupAlarm (risingAlarm(1), fallingAlarm(2) or risingOrFallingAlarm(3)) decides whether a single alarm is generated if the first sample after activation already crosses a threshold.
sections.eli5: The alarm looks at a counter every so often. It rings once when the number climbs past a high line, and rings again only after it has dropped back below that line.

sections.title: Capabilities and Notifications
sections.content:
The capabilities group has a single scalar, hcAlarmCapabilities, which is a set of bits. If hcAlarmCreation is set, the agent lets management applications create entries in the table. If hcAlarmNvStorage is set, the agent supports entries that are recreated after a system restart, as controlled by hcAlarmStorageType.

The two notifications, hcRisingAlarm and hcFallingAlarm, are generated in the same way as RMON-1's risingAlarm and fallingAlarm and convey essentially the same information. They are sent when a crossing generates an event configured for SNMP traps. Each carries the variable, sample type, value, value status, the relevant threshold parts and the event index of the entry that caused it.
sections.eli5: A device can tell the manager whether it can make new alarms and keep them after a restart. When an alarm rings, the message says what was being watched and what the numbers were.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Objects with read-write or read-create access may be sensitive or vulnerable in some environments, and allowing SET operations without proper protection can hurt network operations. The values hcAlarmAbsValue and hcAlarmValueStatus may expose the values of whatever instance hcAlarmVariable points to.

Because SNMP access control is expressed in terms of MIB views, nothing can limit hcAlarmVariable to objects in a particular view. The probe must therefore grant write access to that object only in views that have read access to all objects on the probe. The RFC also warns that SNMPv1 by itself is not a secure environment.
sections.eli5: An alarm can be pointed at any counter, so only people allowed to see everything should be allowed to set one up.

layers.label: eventTable
layers.detail: Shared RMON-1 table that both alarm tables use

layers.label: Notifications
layers.detail: risingAlarm and fallingAlarm, or hcRisingAlarm and hcFallingAlarm
